title: General relativity from a variational principle
one_line_summary: Re-derives Einstein's field equations from an action: proves the Palatini identity for the variation of curvature, shows that coordinate invariance of any action forces a divergence-free Euler-Lagrange tensor (the contracted Bianchi identity), varies sqrt(-g) R both by brute force and by a slicker delta-calculus, explains why the equations stay second order, treats metric and connection as independent (Palatini), and couples matter to define T^ab variationally.
role_in_book: Chapter 10 reached G_ab = kappa T_ab from physical heuristics (lift experiments, geodesic deviation, the Newtonian limit). Chapter 11 deliberately gives a second, purely mathematical route that cashes in the machinery of Part B: geodesic coordinates and the Riemann tensor from Chapter 6, and tensor densities, the metric determinant, the divergence theorem and the Euler-Lagrange equations from Chapter 7. It confirms the vacuum and full equations, shows that the Bianchi identity is a structural consequence of general covariance, and supplies the variational definition of the energy-momentum tensor that Chapter 12 uses for the Maxwell and scalar fields. Its 'trivial' sqrt(-g) Lagrangian reappears as the cosmological term in Chapter 13, and the idea of a quadratic first-derivative Lagrangian returns for linearized gravity in Chapter 21.

assumed_background.topic: Riemann tensor in terms of connection coefficients, with the book's index convention (6.40)
Geodesic coordinates: at a chosen point the connection vanishes so covariant and partial derivatives coincide there
Metric connection, the identity nabla_c g_ab = 0 (6.74) and Exercise 6.21 (a symmetric metric-compatible connection is the Christoffel connection)
Lie derivative of the metric along a vector field and infinitesimal coordinate transformations (7.53)
Tensor densities and weights; covariant divergence of a weight +1 vector density equals the ordinary divergence (7.3)
Metric determinant: derivative of a determinant (7.8), partial derivative of g (7.9), nabla sqrt(-g) = 0 (7.12)
Integration over a region and the divergence (Stokes) theorem for vector densities (7.19)
Euler-Lagrange equations for fields and the variational (functional) derivative notation (7.36)
Einstein tensor, contracted Bianchi identities, vacuum and full field equations G^ab = kappa T^ab (10.54)
A tensor equation valid in one coordinate system is valid in every coordinate system
Hamilton's principle and Lagrangians in classical mechanics, including adding a total time derivative
Integration by parts, multivariable Taylor expansion to first order, continuity arguments
Inverse and determinant of a matrix and their first-order perturbations

learning_objectives: Reader can prove the Palatini identity delta R^a_bcd = nabla_c(delta Gamma^a_bd) - nabla_d(delta Gamma^a_bc) using geodesic coordinates and the tensor character of both sides, and contract it to delta R_bd.
Reader can explain why the difference of two connections is a type (1,2) tensor even though a connection itself is not.

Reader can set up a field-theory action I = integral of a weight +1 scalar density over a region, state the principle of stationary action with variations vanishing on the boundary, and define the Euler-Lagrange tensor density L^ab = delta L / delta g_ab.

Reader can derive the identity nabla_b L^ab = 0 from the invariance of the action under an infinitesimal coordinate change generated by a vector field that vanishes on the boundary, and explain why it holds off-shell.
Reader can compute the Euler-Lagrange derivative of the volume Lagrangian sqrt(-g), obtaining one half of the gothic inverse metric, and explain why it cannot be a physical theory on its own.
Reader can write the Einstein Lagrangian sqrt(-g) R, write the Euler-Lagrange derivative for a Lagrangian containing second derivatives, and state that it yields -sqrt(-g) G^ab.
Reader can use the variation operator as a derivation (linearity and product rule) to show delta g^ab = -g^ac g^bd delta g_cd and delta sqrt(-g) = (1/2) sqrt(-g) g^ab delta g_ab.
Reader can carry out the indirect variation of sqrt(-g) R: use the contracted Palatini identity to turn the delta R_ab term into a boundary term and reduce what remains to the Einstein tensor.

Reader can explain why an action containing second derivatives of the metric still gives second-order field equations, by splitting sqrt(-g) R into a first-order Gamma-Gamma Lagrangian plus a total divergence.
Reader can state why Lagrangians that differ by a total divergence yield identical field equations, and that the Gamma-Gamma Lagrangian is not a scalar density.

Reader can perform the Palatini variation, treating the metric and a symmetric connection as independent, and show that the connection equation forces metric compatibility and hence the Christoffel connection.
Reader can add a matter Lagrangian with coupling 2 kappa, define the energy-momentum tensor as T^ab = (2/sqrt(-g)) delta L_M / delta g_ab, and recover G^ab = kappa T^ab.

teaching_approach.summary: A compact, formula-dense chapter written in the mathematical register of Part B. The authors build a general variational framework for a metric theory, extract what can be learned before choosing any Lagrangian, and only then specialise, first to a toy Lagrangian and then to sqrt(-g) R. The pedagogy is comparative: the same field equations are obtained three ways (brute-force Euler-Lagrange, indirect delta-calculus, Palatini), and each route is chosen to expose a different structural fact (off-shell Bianchi identities, the boundary term, the divergence ambiguity, metric compatibility as an output). Physical motivation is almost absent by design; the physics was done in Chapter 10. Many intermediate steps are handed to the reader as '(exercise)' or '(check)', so the chapter reads as a guided proof outline.
narrative_arc: Forge the key tool first: vary the connection, note the variation is a tensor, and prove the Palatini identity in geodesic coordinates (§11.1).
Set up the general action principle for a metric theory and define the Euler-Lagrange tensor density L^ab (§11.2).
Before choosing any Lagrangian, generate a fake variation by an infinitesimal coordinate change; invariance of I forces nabla_b L^ab = 0 identically (§11.2).
Test the machinery on the simplest density sqrt(-g): the equations are absurd and the identity is trivially true (§11.3).

Move to the next simplest candidate sqrt(-g) R, expand it fully in metric derivatives to show the brute-force route is hopeless, and quote the answer -sqrt(-g) G^ab; the identity becomes the contracted Bianchi identity (§11.4).
Replace brute force with the delta-calculus: product rule, delta of the inverse metric, Palatini identity to push delta R_ab to the boundary, and reduce to G^ab (§11.5).

Confront the puzzle that second derivatives in L should give fourth-order equations; resolve it by splitting off a total divergence and deriving R_ab = 0 from a first-order Gamma-Gamma Lagrangian (§11.6).
Offer the elegant alternative: vary metric and symmetric connection independently; one variation gives the vacuum equations, the other forces the connection to be metric (§11.7).
Add matter, define T^ab variationally with a factor of 2 chosen to match the canonical tensor, and recover the full equations of Chapter 10 (§11.8).
signature_moves: Identities before equations: the constraint nabla_b L^ab = 0 is derived for an unspecified Lagrangian purely from the fact that the action is a scalar, so the Bianchi identity appears as a consequence of general covariance rather than an accident of curvature algebra.

Prove-in-a-special-frame-then-promote: compute at a point in geodesic coordinates where connection terms vanish, then argue that both sides are tensors so the equation holds in all coordinates and at all points.

Show the ugly thing on purpose: the full expansion (11.24) of sqrt(-g) R in metric derivatives is displayed and then abandoned, which motivates the indirect method more convincingly than any assertion.
Warm-up with a deliberately trivial Lagrangian (sqrt(-g)) so that every step of the framework can be checked before the real calculation.
Treat the variation symbol as a derivative-like operator and invite comparison between delta g^ab and the partial-derivative formula (7.9).
Freely swap the choice of dynamical variables (g_ab, g^ab, gothic g^ab, gothic g_ab) to make a calculation tractable, emphasising that the resulting field equations are equivalent.
Pose an apparent paradox (second derivatives in L but second-order equations) and resolve it by a total-divergence decomposition.
Delegate heavy but routine algebra to tagged '(exercise)' prompts that map directly onto end-of-chapter problems.

sections.title: The Palatini equation
sections.summary: Opens without motivation by recalling geodesic coordinates, in which the Riemann tensor at a point reduces to two derivative terms. A connection is perturbed to a nearby connection; their difference is a tensor. The induced change in curvature at the point is written with partial derivatives, which may be swapped for covariant derivatives there. Since both sides are tensors the relation holds in any chart and, the point being arbitrary, everywhere. Contracting gives the variation of the Ricci tensor, the form used repeatedly later.
key_moves: Choose geodesic coordinates at P so Gamma vanishes and R^a_bcd = partial_c Gamma^a_bd - partial_d Gamma^a_bc there (11.1).
Observe that delta Gamma is a difference of two connections and so transforms as a (1,2) tensor.
Commute delta with partial derivatives and replace partial by covariant derivatives at P.
Promote the result to all coordinate systems because both sides are tensors, and to all points because P was arbitrary (11.3).
Contract on a and c to get delta R_bd (11.4).

sections.title: Differential constraints on the field equations
sections.summary: Sets out the action principle for a metric theory: a Lagrangian density of weight +1 built from the metric and its derivatives, integrated over a region; stationarity under boundary-vanishing variations gives field equations L^ab = 0, where L^ab is a symmetric tensor density. Then comes the chapter's most important structural argument: an infinitesimal change of coordinates produces a change in the metric components equal to minus the Lie derivative but cannot change the action. Integrating by parts, discarding a surface term via the divergence theorem, and using the arbitrariness of the region and of the generating vector field yields the identity nabla_b L^ab = 0, valid whether or not the field equations are satisfied.
concepts: metric variation induced by a coordinate change
fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations
key_moves: Require L to be a weight +1 scalar density so the action is coordinate invariant (11.5)-(11.6).
Write the first-order change of the action as the integral of L^ab delta g_ab and conclude L^ab is a symmetric tensor density because delta I is a scalar (11.8)-(11.9).
Generate a variation by x -> x + epsilon X with X vanishing on the boundary; delta g_ab = -epsilon(nabla_b X_a + nabla_a X_b) (11.12)-(11.13).
Use the invariance delta I = 0 identically (11.11) and symmetry of L^ab to reduce to an integral of L^ab nabla_b X_a.
Integrate by parts; the total divergence of the weight +1 density L^ab X_a is an ordinary divergence and becomes a vanishing boundary integral (11.14)-(11.15).
Argue from arbitrary region then arbitrary X that nabla_b L^ab = 0 identically (11.16)-(11.18).

sections.title: A simple example
sections.summary: Introduces the gothic-letter convention (a tensor multiplied by sqrt(-g), hence a weight +1 density) and tries the simplest scalar density built from the metric alone, sqrt(-g). Using the derivative of a determinant, its Euler-Lagrange derivative is half the gothic inverse metric. Setting that to zero is nonsensical as a set of field equations, while the differential identity reduces to a statement already guaranteed by metric compatibility.
key_moves: Define gothic quantities as tensors times sqrt(-g).
Use partial g / partial g_ab = g g^ab (11.20) to get partial sqrt(-g) / partial g_ab = (1/2) gothic g^ab (11.21).
Note gothic g^ab = 0 cannot be field equations, and nabla_b gothic g^ab = 0 is automatically true (11.22).

sections.title: The Einstein Lagrangian
sections.summary: Asserts that the next simplest scalar after the volume element is the Ricci scalar, and takes sqrt(-g) R as the gravitational Lagrangian. Introduces comma notation for partial derivatives and writes the Lagrangian out in full in terms of metric components and their first and second derivatives, making the complexity visible. Gives the Euler-Lagrange derivative for Lagrangians with second derivatives, quotes one of the pieces as an exercise, declines the rest as far too laborious, and states the outcome: the Euler-Lagrange tensor is minus sqrt(-g) times the Einstein tensor, so the vacuum equations follow and the general identity of §11.2 becomes the contracted Bianchi identity.
key_moves: Choose L_G = sqrt(-g) R as the next simplest scalar density (11.23).
Expand R in Christoffel symbols and then in metric derivatives to display the full dependence (11.24).
Generalize the Euler-Lagrange derivative to include a second-derivative term with a plus sign (11.25).
Quote the coefficient of second derivatives (11.26), which contains no metric derivatives.
State L_G^ab = -sqrt(-g) G^ab (11.27), giving G^ab = 0 (11.28) and nabla_b G^ab = 0 (11.29).

sections.title: Indirect derivation of the field equations
sections.summary: Develops a calculus for the variation symbol: it is linear and obeys the product rule. Applying it to the constant Kronecker delta written as g^ab g_bc shows that the variation of the inverse metric is minus the inverse metric twice contracted with the variation of the metric. The action is then written as gothic g^ab R_ab and varied by the product rule. The term containing delta R_ab is rewritten with the contracted Palatini identity; because gothic g^ab is covariantly constant, the integrand is a covariant divergence of a weight +1 vector density and hence a boundary term that drops out. The surviving term, using the variation of sqrt(-g), assembles into minus sqrt(-g) G^ab times delta g_ab, reproducing the field equations and identities in a few lines.
concepts: boundary term in the Einstein-Hilbert variation
key_moves: Vary g^ab g_bc = delta^a_c, which is constant, to get (11.31) and hence delta g^ad = -g^ab g^cd delta g_bc (11.32).
Write I as the integral of gothic g^ab R_ab and apply the product rule (11.33).
Replace delta R_ab by the contracted Palatini identity and pull gothic g^ab inside the covariant derivatives.
Convert the resulting covariant divergence of a vector density into a partial divergence and discard it as a boundary term.
Expand delta gothic g^ab using delta sqrt(-g) (11.35) and delta g^ab, and collect into -sqrt(-g) G^cd delta g_cd (11.34).

sections.title: An equivalent Lagrangian
sections.summary: Addresses why second derivatives in sqrt(-g) R do not produce fourth-order equations: the coefficient of the second derivatives involves only the metric itself and the coefficient of first derivatives involves only first derivatives. To make this explicit, the Einstein Lagrangian is written as a first-order Lagrangian quadratic in the connection coefficients plus a total divergence Q^a_,a. Integrating the derivative-of-Gamma terms by parts and using the expression for derivatives of gothic g^ab in terms of Gamma produces the split. The divergence contributes only a surface term, so both Lagrangians give the same equations, though the first-order one is not a scalar density. Choosing gothic g^ab as the variables, the Euler-Lagrange equations of the Gamma-Gamma Lagrangian reduce, via the identity for the derivative of ln sqrt(-g), to R_ab = 0.
concepts: second-order nature of the Einstein equations
total divergence ambiguity of a Lagrangian
derivative of gothic inverse metric in terms of the connection
contracted connection as gradient of ln sqrt(-g)
key_moves: Point out the puzzle using (11.25) and (11.26).
Expand gothic g^ab R_ab into two derivative-of-Gamma terms minus the quadratic L-bar (11.37)-(11.38).
Integrate by parts to move derivatives onto gothic g^ab, generating the divergence of Q^a (11.39)-(11.40).
Use (11.41), from nabla gothic g^ab = 0, to show the non-divergence pieces sum to L-bar, giving L_G = L-bar + Q^a_,a (11.36).
Treat L-bar as a function of gothic g^ab and its first derivatives; compute its partial derivatives (11.42)-(11.43) and the Euler-Lagrange expression (11.44)-(11.45).
Use Gamma^d_ad = (ln sqrt(-g))_,a (11.46) to symmetrize the derivative terms and recognise R_ab.

sections.title: The Palatini approach
sections.summary: Presents the metric-affine route: the Einstein Lagrangian is regarded as a function of gothic g^ab and of an arbitrary symmetric connection and its first derivatives, with the Ricci tensor built from the connection alone. Varying the metric gives R_ab = 0 at once. Varying the connection, using the contracted Palatini identity and integrating by parts, gives an integrand linear in delta Gamma; because the connection variation is symmetric in its lower indices only the symmetrized coefficient must vanish (11.48). Manipulating this (in an exercise) shows the covariant derivatives of gothic g^ab, sqrt(-g), g^ab and g_ab all vanish, and by Exercise 6.21 a symmetric metric-compatible connection must be the Christoffel connection.
concepts: metric compatibility from the field equations
key_moves: Declare gothic g^ab and a symmetric Gamma to be independent variables in gothic g^ab R_ab(Gamma) (11.47).
Vary gothic g^ab only: delta I = integral of R_ab delta gothic g^ab, so R_ab = 0.
Vary Gamma only: use (11.4), integrate by parts, drop the boundary term.
Rename indices to factor out delta Gamma^c_ab and symmetrize in a and b because delta Gamma is symmetric (11.48).
Deduce nabla_c g_ab = 0 and invoke Exercise 6.21 to identify the Christoffel connection.

sections.title: The full field equations
sections.summary: Adds a matter Lagrangian with a coupling constant, using the combination L_G + 2 kappa L_M. Varying with respect to the metric, the gravitational part gives minus sqrt(-g) G^ab and the matter part is used to define the energy-momentum tensor through T^ab = (2/sqrt(-g)) delta L_M / delta g_ab. The factor of 2 is chosen so that this agrees with the canonical energy-momentum tensor of special relativity (worked out for a scalar field in Exercise 11.13). Dividing by sqrt(-g) gives G^ab = kappa T^ab, matching Chapter 10. The authors note that some texts drop the 2 in both places, and preview Chapter 12.
key_moves: Write the total action as the integral of L_G + 2 kappa L_M (11.49).
Use delta L_G / delta g_ab = -sqrt(-g) G^ab (11.50).
Define T^ab by the metric variation of L_M with a factor 2 (11.51)-(11.52).
Sum, divide by sqrt(-g), obtain G^ab = kappa T^ab (11.53).

concepts.name: geodesic coordinates
aliases: locally inertial coordinates (for the metric connection)
concepts.definition: A coordinate system adapted to a chosen point P in which all connection coefficients vanish at P, so that covariant derivatives equal partial derivatives at that point (though not in a neighbourhood).
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled at the chapter's first line as the standard tool for proving tensor identities; the asterisk-equals notation flags equations valid only in that chart.
concepts.notes: Also suggested as the method for Exercise 11.14 (variation of the connection).

concepts.name: variation of a connection
concepts.definition: The first-order difference delta Gamma^a_bc between a connection and a nearby connection. Although connection coefficients do not transform as a tensor, the inhomogeneous terms cancel in the difference, so delta Gamma^a_bc is a type (1,2) tensor.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced by replacing Gamma with Gamma + delta Gamma; its tensor character is the hinge that lets the Palatini identity be promoted from geodesic coordinates to all coordinates.
concepts.notes: In the metric theory delta Gamma is fixed by delta g_ab (Exercise 11.14); in the Palatini approach it is an independent variation.

concepts.name: Palatini identity
concepts.definition: For any variation of a connection, the change in the Riemann tensor is delta R^a_bcd = nabla_c(delta Gamma^a_bd) - nabla_d(delta Gamma^a_bc), where nabla is the covariant derivative of the unvaried connection.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived at a point in geodesic coordinates where the curvature is a difference of two connection derivatives; partial derivatives commute with variation and equal covariant ones there, and tensor character extends the result everywhere.
concepts.notes: The book derives it in one paragraph; it is then used in §11.5 and §11.7.

concepts.name: contracted Palatini identity
concepts.definition: Contraction of the Palatini identity on its first and third indices: delta R_bd = nabla_a(delta Gamma^a_bd) - nabla_d(delta Gamma^a_ba). Contracted with a covariantly constant density it becomes a total divergence.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained immediately from (11.3) and flagged as the useful form; it is the step that converts the delta R_ab term of the action variation into a boundary integral.

concepts.name: tensor equation invariance
aliases: a tensor identity in one chart holds in all charts
concepts.definition: If an equation between tensors holds in one coordinate system at a point, it holds in every coordinate system at that point, because both sides transform identically.
concepts.how_introduced: Invoked as the 'fundamental result' that lets a geodesic-coordinate computation become a general identity.

concepts.name: Lagrangian density
concepts.definition: A scalar density of weight +1 built from the dynamical fields (here the metric and its first and possibly higher derivatives) whose integral over a region with the coordinate volume element is coordinate invariant.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated as the starting specification of the variational principle; the weight +1 requirement is justified by the need for an invariant action integral.

concepts.name: action integral
concepts.definition: The integral I of a Lagrangian density over a region Omega of the manifold with the coordinate volume element dOmega; its stationarity under suitable variations defines the field equations.
concepts.how_introduced: Formed right after the Lagrangian density is required to be weight +1.

concepts.name: principle of stationary action
concepts.definition: The physical field configuration is one for which the action does not change to first order under arbitrary variations of the dynamical variables that vanish on the boundary of the region.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated formally in the variational notation of Chapter 7 as the demand delta I = 0 for all boundary-vanishing delta g_ab.
concepts.notes: The chapter does not discuss how much of the variation (value versus normal derivatives) must vanish on the boundary when L contains second derivatives.

concepts.name: Euler-Lagrange derivative
concepts.definition: The quantity L^ab = delta L / delta g_ab defined so that the first-order change of the action is the integral of L^ab delta g_ab; for Lagrangians depending on derivatives it equals the partial derivative minus the divergence of the first-derivative coefficient plus the double divergence of the second-derivative coefficient. For a metric theory it is a symmetric tensor density of weight +1.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined abstractly in §11.2; its tensor-density character is inferred from delta I being a scalar; generalized to second derivatives in (11.25).

concepts.name: diffeomorphism invariance of the action
concepts.definition: Because the Lagrangian is a scalar density, an infinitesimal relabelling of coordinates inside a region changes the metric components but leaves the action exactly unchanged, so the induced first-order change of I vanishes identically.
concepts.how_introduced: Used as a device: a coordinate change is treated as a 'variation' of g_ab, turning invariance into delta I = 0 identically.
concepts.notes: This is the content of Noether's second theorem, although the book does not name it.

concepts.name: metric variation induced by a coordinate change
concepts.definition: Under x^a -> x^a + epsilon X^a, the new metric components evaluated at the same coordinate values differ from the old by minus the Lie derivative: delta g_ab = -epsilon(nabla_a X_b + nabla_b X_a).
concepts.how_introduced: Quoted with reference to the isometry calculation of §7.7 and left as Exercise 11.1.
concepts.notes: The same combination set to zero is Killing's equation from §7.7.

concepts.name: divergence theorem for vector densities
aliases: integration by parts in the action
concepts.definition: For a weight +1 vector density the covariant divergence equals the ordinary divergence, and its integral over a region equals the flux through the boundary; if the density vanishes on the boundary the integral is zero.
concepts.how_introduced: Used three times (§11.2, §11.5, §11.7) as 'the usual argument' for discarding total divergences.

concepts.name: fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations
concepts.definition: If a continuous function integrates to zero over every region, it vanishes everywhere; and if W^a X_a = 0 for arbitrary X_a then W^a = 0.
concepts.how_introduced: Used as the final two steps of the identity derivation, with proofs deferred to Exercise 11.8 (continuity and choice of test vectors).

concepts.name: generalized Bianchi identity
concepts.definition: For any metric Lagrangian that is a scalar density, the Euler-Lagrange tensor density is covariantly divergence-free identically, i.e. whether or not the field equations hold.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived before any Lagrangian is chosen, from coordinate invariance of the action; later specialised to sqrt(-g) (trivial) and sqrt(-g) R (contracted Bianchi identity).
prerequisites: metric variation induced by a coordinate change
fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations
concepts.notes: Exercise 11.7 asks what the analogous identity is for other choices of dynamical variable.

concepts.name: contracted Bianchi identities
concepts.definition: The Einstein tensor has identically vanishing covariant divergence.
concepts.how_introduced: Reappears here as the special case of the generalized identity for the Einstein Lagrangian, giving a covariance-based explanation of a result first obtained from curvature algebra.

concepts.name: gothic tensor density notation
concepts.definition: A tensor written in gothic (fraktur) type denotes the ordinary tensor multiplied by sqrt(-g), making it a tensor density of weight +1, e.g. gothic g^ab = sqrt(-g) g^ab.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced at the start of §11.3 to shorten all later formulas.

concepts.name: volume Lagrangian sqrt(-g)
concepts.definition: The Lagrangian consisting of the invariant volume density sqrt(-g) alone; its Euler-Lagrange derivative is (1/2) sqrt(-g) g^ab, so on its own it gives the impossible equation g^ab = 0.
concepts.how_introduced: Offered as the simplest possible test of the framework; the resulting identity is trivially true by metric compatibility.
concepts.notes: Not stated here, but DIV ch13 §13.3 adds 2 Lambda sqrt(-g) to the Einstein Lagrangian to obtain the cosmological term, citing §11.3.

concepts.name: derivative of the metric determinant
concepts.definition: Treating the metric components as independent variables, partial g / partial g_ab = g g^ab; hence the variation of sqrt(-g) is one half sqrt(-g) g^ab delta g_ab.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from (7.8) in §11.3 and used again as (11.35) in the indirect derivation.

concepts.name: Einstein-Hilbert Lagrangian
concepts.definition: The gravitational Lagrangian density L_G = sqrt(-g) R, equivalently gothic g^ab R_ab. It depends on the metric and its first and second derivatives, and its Euler-Lagrange derivative with respect to g_ab is -sqrt(-g) G^ab.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as the next simplest scalar density after sqrt(-g); first expanded brute force (11.24), then varied indirectly (§11.5), rewritten as first order (§11.6) and treated in Palatini form (§11.7).
concepts.notes: The book calls it the Einstein Lagrangian and does not name Hilbert in this chapter (Hilbert's 1915 variational derivation is mentioned in ch13 §13.3).

concepts.name: comma notation
concepts.definition: A comma followed by an index denotes partial differentiation, e.g. g_ab,c = partial_c g_ab, which keeps derivatives of Lagrangians with respect to derivatives of fields readable.
concepts.how_introduced: Adopted at the start of the Einstein Lagrangian calculation to avoid writing partial L / partial(partial_c g_ab).

concepts.name: Euler-Lagrange derivative with second derivatives
concepts.definition: For a Lagrangian depending on a field, its first and its second derivatives, the variational derivative has an extra term: the double divergence of the partial derivative of L with respect to the second derivatives, entering with a plus sign.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated as a generalization of the first-order form (7.36) once sqrt(-g) R is recognised to contain second derivatives.

concepts.name: vacuum field equations
concepts.definition: In the absence of matter the Einstein tensor vanishes; taking the trace shows this is the same as a vanishing Ricci tensor in any dimension other than two.
concepts.how_introduced: Recovered three times as the Euler-Lagrange equations: G^ab = 0 from the metric variation (§11.4-§11.5), R_ab = 0 from the Gamma-Gamma Lagrangian with gothic g^ab variables (§11.6), and R_ab = 0 in the Palatini form (§11.7).

concepts.name: variation as a derivation
aliases: delta obeys linearity and the Leibniz rule
concepts.definition: The first-order variation operator delta acts on sums and products like a derivative: it is linear with constant coefficients and satisfies delta(L1 L2) = L1 delta L2 + L2 delta L1; it also commutes with partial differentiation.
concepts.how_introduced: Announced at the start of §11.5 (proof in Exercise 11.5) and demonstrated on the constant Kronecker delta.

concepts.name: variation of the inverse metric
concepts.definition: A change delta g_ab of the metric induces delta g^ab = -g^ac g^bd delta g_cd in the inverse metric: the indices are raised with a minus sign.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by varying g^ab g_bc = delta^a_c, which cannot change, and multiplying through by the inverse metric; the reader is asked to compare with the partial-derivative formula (7.9).
concepts.notes: Exercise 11.3 gives the corresponding partial-derivative formula with explicit symmetrization.

concepts.name: boundary term in the Einstein-Hilbert variation
concepts.definition: The part of the action variation proportional to delta R_ab equals the integral of an ordinary divergence of a vector density built from gothic g^ab and delta Gamma, which converts to a surface integral and is discarded when variations vanish on the boundary.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived in §11.5 by combining the contracted Palatini identity with the covariant constancy of gothic g^ab and (7.3).
concepts.notes: Because delta Gamma contains first derivatives of delta g_ab, discarding this term strictly requires those derivatives to vanish on the boundary too; the modern fix is the Gibbons-Hawking-York term, which the book does not discuss.

concepts.name: second-order nature of the Einstein equations
concepts.definition: Although sqrt(-g) R contains second derivatives of the metric, the Euler-Lagrange equations are only second order, because the coefficient of the second derivatives depends only on g_ab and the first-derivative coefficient only on first derivatives, so the potentially fourth-order terms cancel.
concepts.how_introduced: Raised as a surprise in §11.6 with reference to (11.25)-(11.26) and made manifest by the total-divergence split.

concepts.name: total divergence ambiguity of a Lagrangian
concepts.definition: Two Lagrangians that differ by a total divergence Q^a_,a give the same Euler-Lagrange equations, since the divergence integrates to a boundary term that does not affect the variation.
concepts.how_introduced: Asserted in §11.6 and proved for the one-variable mechanics case in Exercise 11.9; it justifies replacing sqrt(-g) R by the first-order Gamma-Gamma Lagrangian.

concepts.name: Gamma-Gamma Lagrangian
concepts.definition: The Lagrangian formed by contracting gothic g^ab with the difference of the two possible index-linked products of Christoffel symbols (see formulas), quadratic in connection coefficients and so depending only on the metric and its first derivatives. It differs from sqrt(-g) R by a total divergence and is not a scalar density.
concepts.how_introduced: Extracted from the expansion of gothic g^ab R_ab by integrating the derivative-of-Gamma terms by parts; then used with gothic g^ab as dynamical variables to derive R_ab = 0.
prerequisites: total divergence ambiguity of a Lagrangian
derivative of gothic inverse metric in terms of the connection
concepts.notes: Not a scalar density, so the generalized identity of §11.2 does not directly apply to it.

concepts.name: choice of dynamical variables
aliases: g_ab vs g^ab vs gothic variables
concepts.definition: The same Lagrangian may be regarded as a function of g_ab, g^ab, gothic g^ab or gothic g_ab (and their derivatives); the Euler-Lagrange derivatives differ by invertible algebraic factors, so the field equations are equivalent, but one choice can make the algebra much simpler.
concepts.how_introduced: Noted in §11.4 and §11.6, exploited with gothic g^ab in §11.6-§11.7, and systematised in Exercise 11.7 (giving R_ab, -R^ab and sqrt(-g) G_ab).

concepts.name: derivative of gothic inverse metric in terms of the connection
concepts.definition: Because the covariant derivative of the weight +1 density gothic g^ab vanishes, its partial derivative can be written purely with connection coefficients: gothic g^ab_,c = Gamma^d_dc gothic g^ab - Gamma^a_dc gothic g^db - Gamma^b_dc gothic g^ad.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated as an exercise in §11.6 and used to show the non-divergence part of sqrt(-g) R equals the Gamma-Gamma Lagrangian.

concepts.name: contracted connection as gradient of ln sqrt(-g)
concepts.definition: For the metric connection the contraction Gamma^d_ad equals the partial derivative of ln sqrt(-g), so its further partial derivative is symmetric in the two derivative indices.
concepts.how_introduced: Quoted as an exercise at the end of §11.6 to symmetrize the derivative terms in the Euler-Lagrange expression and recognise the Ricci tensor.

concepts.name: Palatini (metric-affine) variation
concepts.definition: A variational method in which the metric (here gothic g^ab) and a symmetric connection are independent dynamical variables in L = gothic g^ab R_ab(Gamma); the metric variation gives the vacuum equations and the connection variation determines the connection.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as the elegant alternative after the metric-only routes; relies again on the contracted Palatini identity and integration by parts.
concepts.notes: With a non-symmetric connection the method leaves a projective freedom and torsion issues; the book avoids this by assuming symmetry.

concepts.name: symmetric connection
concepts.definition: An affine connection whose coefficients are symmetric in their two lower indices, Gamma^a_bc = Gamma^a_cb.
concepts.how_introduced: Assumed from the start in the Palatini approach; the symmetry of delta Gamma means only the symmetric part of its coefficient is forced to vanish.

concepts.name: metric compatibility from the field equations
aliases: connection equation of the Palatini method
concepts.definition: In the Palatini variation, stationarity with respect to an arbitrary symmetric connection yields equations whose only solution (in any dimension above two) is nabla_c g_ab = 0, so the metric connection is derived rather than assumed.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained from (11.48) through a chain of deductions for gothic g^ab, sqrt(-g), g^ab and g_ab (Exercise 11.11), closed by Exercise 6.21.
concepts.notes: The step from nabla gothic g^ab = 0 to nabla sqrt(-g) = 0 uses the determinant of gothic g^ab, which fails in two dimensions (own observation).

concepts.name: metric connection
concepts.definition: The unique symmetric connection with nabla_c g_ab = 0, whose coefficients are half the inverse metric contracted with the usual three-term combination of first metric derivatives (the Christoffel symbols of the second kind).
concepts.how_introduced: Appears as the output of the Palatini connection variation via Exercise 6.21.

concepts.name: matter Lagrangian
concepts.definition: A Lagrangian density describing non-gravitational fields, depending on the metric and its derivatives as well as the matter fields, added to the gravitational Lagrangian with coupling 2 kappa.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced in §11.8 to extend the vacuum treatment to the full field equations.

concepts.name: coupling constant
concepts.definition: The constant kappa multiplying the matter contribution in the action and appearing in G^ab = kappa T^ab (equal to 8 pi G / c^4, or 8 pi in relativistic units, per Chapter 10).
concepts.how_introduced: Used without numerical discussion; the factor of 2 accompanying it is explained by the normalization of T^ab.
concepts.notes: The numerical value is fixed in DIV ch10 and ch12 §12.3.

concepts.name: variational (Hilbert) energy-momentum tensor
aliases: T^ab from delta L_M / delta g_ab
concepts.definition: The energy-momentum tensor defined from the metric variation of the matter Lagrangian: T^ab = (2/sqrt(-g)) delta L_M / delta g_ab, equivalently sqrt(-g) T_ab = -2 delta L_M / delta g^ab.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined in §11.8 so that the combined Euler-Lagrange equations become G^ab = kappa T^ab; the 2 is justified by agreement with the canonical tensor of special relativity (Exercise 11.13).
concepts.notes: Chapter 12 applies this route to the Maxwell and scalar fields.

concepts.name: full field equations
concepts.definition: The Einstein tensor equals the coupling constant times the energy-momentum tensor of all non-gravitational fields.
concepts.how_introduced: Recovered from the combined action, in agreement with (10.54).

concepts.name: canonical energy-momentum tensor
concepts.definition: In special relativity, for a field Lagrangian L(phi, partial phi), the tensor built from the derivative of L with respect to the field gradients times the gradient, plus delta^a_b L (with the book's sign convention a minus sign on the first term).
concepts.how_introduced: Appears only in Exercise 11.13, where it is shown to coincide with the variational T_ab for a scalar field in flat spacetime, justifying the factor of 2.

concepts.name: minimal coupling
concepts.definition: Carrying a special-relativistic Lagrangian into curved spacetime by replacing eta by g, partial by covariant derivatives and multiplying by sqrt(-g), without adding explicit curvature terms.
concepts.how_introduced: Invoked only in Exercise 11.13 to build the curved-spacetime scalar-field Lagrangian density.

concepts.name: Eddington quadratic Lagrangian
concepts.definition: A higher-curvature action, sqrt(-g) times the full contraction of the Riemann tensor with itself, which Eddington considered as an alternative to sqrt(-g) R.
concepts.how_introduced: Set as Exercise 11.12, to be varied treating g^ab and R^abcd as independent.
concepts.notes: The book gives no answer. Own note: varied as a function of the metric alone, a curvature-squared action gives fourth-order field equations. The exercise's instruction to treat R^abcd as independent is what keeps the calculation manageable.

concepts.name: variation of the connection in terms of the metric
concepts.definition: For the metric connection, a metric variation induces a change in Gamma that has the same three-term structure as the Christoffel formula, but with partial derivatives of g replaced by covariant derivatives of delta g; it is therefore a tensor.
concepts.how_introduced: Set as Exercise 11.14, to be proved by the geodesic-coordinate method of §11.1, as preparation for matter Lagrangians containing covariant derivatives.

key_equations.name: Riemann tensor in geodesic coordinates
key_equations.meaning: At a point where the connection vanishes, curvature is just the antisymmetrized derivative of the connection; the quadratic terms of (6.40) drop out.
key_equations.symbols: asterisk: valid only in geodesic coordinates at P

key_equations.name: Varied connection
key_equations.meaning: A nearby connection; the difference delta Gamma is a (1,2) tensor.

key_equations.name: Variation of curvature at P
key_equations.meaning: Variation commutes with partial derivatives, which equal covariant derivatives at P in geodesic coordinates.

key_equations.name: Palatini identity
key_equations.meaning: The first-order change in the Riemann tensor is a covariant 'curl' of the change in the connection; valid in all coordinates since both sides are tensors.
key_equations.symbols: nabla: covariant derivative of the unvaried connection

key_equations.name: Contracted Palatini identity
key_equations.meaning: Variation of the Ricci tensor, obtained by contracting a with c; used to turn the delta R_ab contribution to the action into a divergence.

key_equations.name: Lagrangian dependence
key_equations.meaning: The Lagrangian density is a function of the metric and its derivatives.

key_equations.name: Action
key_equations.meaning: Integral of the weight +1 scalar density over a region; coordinate invariant.
key_equations.symbols: Omega: region; dOmega: coordinate volume element

key_equations.name: Stationary action
key_equations.latex: g_{ab}\to g_{ab}+\delta g_{ab}\ \Rightarrow\ I\to I+\delta I\ \text{with}\ \delta I = 0
key_equations.meaning: For metric variations vanishing on the boundary, the action does not change to first order.

key_equations.name: First variation of the action
key_equations.meaning: The change of the action is linear in delta g_ab with coefficient L^ab (after discarding boundary terms).

key_equations.name: Euler-Lagrange tensor density
key_equations.meaning: Definition of the variational derivative; it is a symmetric tensor density of weight +1.

key_equations.name: Field equations
key_equations.meaning: The field equations of the theory are the vanishing of the Euler-Lagrange derivative.

key_equations.name: Invariance under coordinate change
key_equations.meaning: If the 'variation' is produced by a coordinate change, the action is unchanged identically, not just on solutions.

key_equations.name: Infinitesimal coordinate change
key_equations.meaning: Generator X^a is a smooth vector field vanishing on the boundary of Omega.

key_equations.name: Metric change under coordinate change
key_equations.latex: \delta g_{ab} = g'_{ab}(x) - g_{ab}(x) = -\mathrm{L}_{\varepsilon X}g_{ab} = -\varepsilon(\nabla_b X_a + \nabla_a X_b)
key_equations.meaning: Comparing new and old metric components at the same coordinate values gives minus the Lie derivative, i.e. the symmetrized covariant derivative of X.
key_equations.symbols: L_{epsilon X}: Lie derivative along epsilon X

key_equations.name: Identity in integral form
key_equations.meaning: Substituting (11.13) into (11.8) and using symmetry of L^ab.

key_equations.name: Integration by parts
key_equations.meaning: Leibniz rule for covariant derivatives splits the integral into a bulk term and a total divergence.

key_equations.name: Divergence to surface term
key_equations.meaning: The covariant divergence of a weight +1 vector density is an ordinary divergence; the divergence theorem makes it a boundary flux, which vanishes since X does.
Remaining bulk integral vanishes for every region.
Arbitrariness of Omega removes the integral (Exercise 11.8(i)).

key_equations.name: Generalized Bianchi identity
key_equations.meaning: The Euler-Lagrange tensor of any covariant metric Lagrangian is identically divergence-free; four differential constraints on the ten field equations.

key_equations.name: Gothic densities
key_equations.meaning: Gothic letters denote tensors multiplied by sqrt(-g), which are weight +1 densities.

key_equations.name: Volume Lagrangian
key_equations.meaning: Simplest scalar density built from the metric alone.

key_equations.name: Derivative of the determinant
key_equations.meaning: From (7.8): the cofactor of g_ab is g g^ab.
Chain rule applied to sqrt(-g).

key_equations.name: Euler-Lagrange derivative of sqrt(-g)
key_equations.meaning: No derivative terms, so the variational derivative is the partial derivative; setting it to zero is impossible.
The identity for the volume Lagrangian, automatically satisfied by (6.74) and (7.12).

key_equations.name: Einstein Lagrangian
key_equations.meaning: Gravitational Lagrangian density; subscript G for gravitation.

key_equations.name: Einstein Lagrangian expanded
key_equations.meaning: Written out fully in the book (four bracketed lines) to show explicit dependence on g_ab, g_ab,c and g_ab,cd and hence the forbidding complexity of brute-force variation.

key_equations.name: Dependence of L_G
key_equations.meaning: g^ab and g are regarded as functions of g_ab.

key_equations.name: Euler-Lagrange derivative with second derivatives
key_equations.meaning: Generalization of (7.36); the last term naively threatens fourth-order equations.

key_equations.name: Second-derivative coefficient
key_equations.meaning: Contains no derivatives of the metric, which is why the double divergence term in (11.25) is only second order.
key_equations.symbols: Printed with delta rather than partial on the left; the partial derivative is meant (cf. Exercise 11.2)

key_equations.name: Variational derivative of the Einstein Lagrangian
key_equations.meaning: The Euler-Lagrange tensor of sqrt(-g) R is minus the densitized Einstein tensor.

key_equations.name: Vacuum field equations
key_equations.meaning: Euler-Lagrange equations of the Einstein Lagrangian.

key_equations.name: Contracted Bianchi identities from covariance
key_equations.meaning: The generalized identity (11.18) specialised to L_G, using nabla sqrt(-g) = 0.

key_equations.name: Induced variation of inverse metric
key_equations.meaning: Varying g_ab changes g^ab too.

key_equations.name: Varying the Kronecker delta
key_equations.latex: \delta^a_c = g^{ab}g_{bc} \to (g^{ab}+\delta g^{ab})(g_{bc}+\delta g_{bc}) = \delta^a_c + \delta g^{ab}g_{bc} + g^{ab}\delta g_{bc} + O(\delta^2)
key_equations.meaning: Expanding the product to first order.
The constant Kronecker delta cannot vary.

key_equations.name: Variation of the inverse metric
key_equations.meaning: Raising indices on delta g_bc introduces a minus sign; compare with the partial-derivative relation (7.9).

key_equations.name: Action in gothic form
key_equations.meaning: Starting point of the indirect derivation.

key_equations.name: Product rule on the action
key_equations.meaning: Splits the variation into a metric-variation term and a curvature-variation term.

key_equations.name: Curvature-variation term is a divergence
key_equations.meaning: Using (11.4), nabla gothic g^ab = 0 and (7.3); the result is a boundary term that is discarded.

key_equations.name: Indirect variation of the Einstein action
key_equations.latex: \delta I = \int_\Omega R_{ab}\,\delta\mathfrak{g}^{ab}\,\mathrm{d}\Omega = \int_\Omega\sqrt{-g}\big(\tfrac12 R g^{cd} - R_{ab}g^{ac}g^{bd}\big)\delta g_{cd}\,\mathrm{d}\Omega = \int_\Omega[-\sqrt{-g}\,G^{ab}]\,\delta g_{ab}\,\mathrm{d}\Omega
key_equations.meaning: After dropping the boundary term, expanding delta(sqrt(-g) g^ab) yields minus sqrt(-g) times the Einstein tensor, reproducing (11.27) with little effort.

key_equations.name: Variation of sqrt(-g)
key_equations.meaning: Variational analogue of (11.21); Exercise 11.6(iii).

key_equations.name: Einstein Lagrangian as first-order Lagrangian plus divergence
key_equations.meaning: sqrt(-g) R differs from a Lagrangian containing only first metric derivatives by a total divergence, so both give the same field equations.
key_equations.symbols: L-bar_G: first-order Lagrangian; Q^a: divergence vector

key_equations.meaning: Separates the derivative-of-connection terms from the quadratic terms.

key_equations.name: Gamma-Gamma Lagrangian
key_equations.meaning: First-order Lagrangian for gravity: quadratic in Christoffel symbols, not a scalar density.
Integration by parts moves the derivatives off the connection onto gothic g^ab.

key_equations.name: Divergence vector
key_equations.meaning: The quantity whose divergence is discarded.

key_equations.name: Partial derivative of gothic inverse metric
key_equations.meaning: Restatement of nabla_c gothic g^ab = 0; substituting it into (11.39) turns the first two terms into 2 L-bar_G.

key_equations.name: L-bar as function of gothic variables
key_equations.meaning: Choice of dynamical variables for the first-order Lagrangian (the reading copy's OCR drops the comma).
Partial derivative with respect to the undifferentiated variable (derived in Exercise 11.10(vi)).
Partial derivative with respect to first derivatives; symmetrized in a,b because gothic g^ab_,c is symmetric.

key_equations.name: Euler-Lagrange equations of L-bar
key_equations.meaning: Ordinary first-order Euler-Lagrange form.
Combining (11.42) and (11.43).

key_equations.name: Contracted connection as log-gradient
key_equations.meaning: Makes Gamma^d_ad,b symmetric in a and b.

key_equations.name: Symmetry of contracted connection derivative
key_equations.meaning: Partial derivatives commute.

key_equations.name: First-order Lagrangian gives Ricci
key_equations.meaning: With gothic g^ab as variables the field equations are R_ab = 0.

key_equations.name: Palatini Lagrangian
key_equations.meaning: Same Lagrangian, but Gamma is now an independent symmetric connection, so R_ab depends on Gamma alone.

key_equations.name: Palatini metric variation
key_equations.meaning: Varying only the metric gives R_ab = 0 immediately.

key_equations.name: Palatini connection variation
key_equations.meaning: After using (11.4) and integrating by parts; the integrand must vanish, but the printed line omits '= 0'.

key_equations.name: Palatini connection equation
key_equations.meaning: Only the part symmetric in a,b survives since delta Gamma^c_ab is symmetric; it implies nabla_c g_ab = 0.

key_equations.name: Metric connection
key_equations.meaning: The unique symmetric metric-compatible connection (Exercise 6.21).

key_equations.name: Total action with matter
key_equations.meaning: Gravity plus matter; factor 2 fixes the normalization of T^ab.
key_equations.symbols: kappa: coupling constant; L_M: matter Lagrangian

key_equations.meaning: Restates (11.27).
Metric variation of the matter Lagrangian, used as a definition.

key_equations.name: Variational energy-momentum tensor
key_equations.meaning: Defines the energy-momentum tensor of any matter fields from their Lagrangian; agrees with the canonical tensor in flat spacetime.

key_equations.name: Full field equations
key_equations.meaning: Einstein's equations recovered from the action, matching (10.54).

key_equations.label: Ex. 11.3
key_equations.name: Partial derivative of inverse metric
key_equations.meaning: Symmetrized partial-derivative version of (11.32).

key_equations.label: Ex. 11.6
key_equations.name: Variations of determinant quantities
key_equations.latex: g_{ab}\delta g^{ab} = -g^{ab}\delta g_{ab},\quad \delta g = g\,g^{ab}\delta g_{ab},\quad \delta\sqrt{-g} = \tfrac12\sqrt{-g}\,g^{ab}\delta g_{ab}
key_equations.meaning: Toolkit for the indirect derivation.

key_equations.label: Ex. 11.7
key_equations.name: Euler-Lagrange derivatives for other variables
key_equations.meaning: Different choices of variable give algebraically equivalent field equations.

key_equations.label: Ex. 11.13
key_equations.name: Scalar field Lagrangian and canonical tensor
key_equations.latex: L = -\tfrac12 g^{cd}\phi_{,c}\phi_{,d} + V(\phi),\quad \Theta^a{}_b := -\frac{\partial L}{\partial(\phi_{,a})}\phi_{,b} + \delta^a_b L,\quad \Theta_{00} = \tfrac12(\dot\phi^2 + |\nabla\phi|^2) + V(\phi)
key_equations.meaning: Flat-space check that the variational T_ab equals the canonical tensor; the sign of L is adapted to signature (+,-,-,-) and the book's action conventions.

key_equations.label: Ex. 11.14
key_equations.name: Variation of the metric connection
key_equations.meaning: Needed when matter Lagrangians contain covariant derivatives.

worked_examples.label: Inline derivation §11.1: Palatini identity
worked_examples.problem: Find the first-order change in the Riemann tensor when the connection is perturbed.
worked_examples.method: Work at an arbitrary point in geodesic coordinates, where the curvature is the antisymmetrized derivative of Gamma; vary, swap partial for covariant derivatives at the point, then use the tensor character of delta Gamma and delta R to extend the equation to all charts and points; contract.
worked_examples.key_insight: A calculation that looks coordinate dependent becomes a general identity once every object in it is shown to be a tensor.

worked_examples.label: Inline derivation §11.2: identities from coordinate invariance
worked_examples.problem: Show that for any metric Lagrangian that is a scalar density, the Euler-Lagrange tensor density obeys four differential identities.
worked_examples.method: Induce delta g_ab by an infinitesimal coordinate change generated by X vanishing on the boundary; the action is unchanged; substitute the Lie-derivative formula, integrate by parts, convert the divergence of a weight +1 density to a surface integral that vanishes, and apply the arbitrariness of Omega and of X.
worked_examples.key_insight: The identities follow from covariance alone and hold off-shell; for GR they are the contracted Bianchi identities, so ten field equations carry four built-in constraints.

worked_examples.label: Inline example §11.3: the Lagrangian sqrt(-g)
worked_examples.problem: Compute the field equations and identities for the Lagrangian consisting only of sqrt(-g).
worked_examples.method: Differentiate the determinant using (7.8), apply the chain rule, and substitute into the general identity.
worked_examples.key_insight: The machinery works but this Lagrangian alone is physically empty; it is a harmless consistency check of the identity.

worked_examples.label: Inline calculation §11.4: brute-force Einstein Lagrangian
worked_examples.problem: Attempt the Euler-Lagrange derivative of sqrt(-g) R directly as a function of g_ab and its first and second derivatives.
worked_examples.method: Expand R in Christoffel symbols and those in metric derivatives (11.24), write the second-order Euler-Lagrange expression (11.25), and compute the second-derivative coefficient (11.26); the remaining pieces are skipped and the final answer quoted.
worked_examples.key_insight: Displaying the expansion makes the case for a smarter method; the one computed coefficient already hints that the equations will be only second order.

worked_examples.label: Inline derivation §11.5: variation of the inverse metric
worked_examples.problem: Express delta g^ab in terms of delta g_ab.
worked_examples.method: Vary the identity g^ab g_bc = delta^a_c to first order using the product rule and multiply by g^cd.
worked_examples.key_insight: Constants have zero variation; the inverse relation introduces a minus sign, just like the derivative of a matrix inverse.

worked_examples.label: Inline derivation §11.5: field equations by the indirect method
worked_examples.problem: Derive the vacuum field equations from sqrt(-g) R without brute force.
worked_examples.method: Write the action as gothic g^ab R_ab; product rule; replace delta R_ab by (11.4) and use nabla gothic g^ab = 0 to form a total divergence that becomes a boundary term; expand delta(sqrt(-g) g^ab) with (11.35) and (11.32); collect into the Einstein tensor.
worked_examples.key_insight: The Palatini identity isolates all derivatives of the variation into a surface term, leaving an algebraic coefficient of delta g_ab.
concepts: boundary term in the Einstein-Hilbert variation

worked_examples.label: Inline derivation §11.6: first-order Lagrangian
worked_examples.problem: Show sqrt(-g) R equals a first-order Lagrangian plus a divergence, and derive the field equations from the first-order Lagrangian.
worked_examples.method: Split gothic g^ab R_ab into derivative-of-Gamma terms and quadratic terms; integrate by parts to generate Q^a_,a; use (11.41) to turn the remaining pieces into L-bar_G; then treat L-bar_G as a function of gothic g^ab and its first derivatives, compute (11.42)-(11.43), form the Euler-Lagrange expression and simplify with (11.46).
worked_examples.key_insight: The apparent second derivatives in the Einstein Lagrangian sit entirely inside a total divergence, which is why the equations are second order.
concepts: total divergence ambiguity of a Lagrangian
second-order nature of the Einstein equations

worked_examples.label: Inline derivation §11.7: Palatini variation
worked_examples.problem: Vary gothic g^ab R_ab(Gamma) independently with respect to the metric and a symmetric connection.
worked_examples.method: Metric variation gives R_ab = 0 immediately. For the connection, apply (11.4), integrate by parts, relabel to factor out delta Gamma^c_ab, symmetrize in a,b, and deduce successively that gothic g^ab, sqrt(-g), g^ab and g_ab are covariantly constant; Exercise 6.21 then fixes Gamma.
worked_examples.key_insight: The Levi-Civita connection is an equation of motion of the first-order action rather than an assumption.
concepts: metric compatibility from the field equations

worked_examples.label: Inline derivation §11.8: coupling matter
worked_examples.problem: Obtain the full field equations from a combined gravitational and matter action.
worked_examples.method: Vary the integral of L_G + 2 kappa L_M with respect to g_ab, define T^ab from the matter variation, and divide by sqrt(-g).
worked_examples.key_insight: The energy-momentum tensor can be defined as the response of the matter action to a change of metric; the factor 2 makes it agree with the canonical tensor.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: The variation symbol behaves like a derivative (linear, Leibniz rule), so delta g^ab mirrors the formula for differentiating an inverse matrix.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: The authors apply the product rule to g^ab g_bc = delta^a_c and explicitly ask the reader to compare the result with the partial-derivative relation (7.9).
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Variation acts on the space of field configurations at fixed coordinates, not along a direction in spacetime; it commutes with partial derivatives but is not itself a derivative with respect to a coordinate.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Matrix sandbox: learner perturbs a 4x4 symmetric metric with a small random symmetric matrix, and the app shows the exact change in the inverse and in sqrt(-g) beside the first-order predictions -g^-1 dg g^-1 and (1/2) sqrt(-g) tr(g^-1 dg), with the error shrinking quadratically as the perturbation slider is reduced.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: A coordinate change as a 'variation' that cannot change anything physical
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Relabelling points inside a region alters the numbers g_ab but not the action, so the Euler-Lagrange tensor must be orthogonal to every such change; this yields the identity without knowing L.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The argument needs the Lagrangian to be a true scalar density; it does not apply directly to the non-covariant Gamma-Gamma Lagrangian of §11.6.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Show a 2D region with a coordinate grid and a metric-coloured field; the learner drags a bump vector field X (zero at the boundary) that warps the grid; component plots of g_ab change visibly while an 'action' readout stays fixed.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Proving an identity in a convenient frame, then promoting it: compute where the connection vanishes, then let tensor transformation carry the result everywhere
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Geodesic coordinates kill the quadratic Gamma terms; since delta Gamma and delta R are tensors, the simplified equation is automatically general.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Works only for equations whose every term is a tensor; derivatives of the connection itself are not tensors and cannot be promoted.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: A two-panel proof card: left shows a general chart with all Gamma terms visible; toggling 'geodesic coordinates at P' greys out the Gamma terms and highlights which surviving objects are tensors, with a check mark lighting up for each before the 'valid everywhere' badge appears.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Adding a total time derivative to a mechanical Lagrangian does not change the equations of motion
analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: total divergence ambiguity of a Lagrangian
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Exercise 11.9 reduces the field-theory statement L_G = L-bar_G + Q^a_,a to the familiar one-dimensional version with dQ/dx.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: In field theory the boundary term can matter for the well-posedness of the variational problem and for energy definitions, even though bulk equations are unchanged.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Pendulum plotter: the learner types an extra function Q(theta, t); the app shows the Lagrangian curve change while the computed trajectory from the Euler-Lagrange equation stays identical.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Letting the action choose the connection, like letting a variational principle choose a path
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: The Palatini approach treats the connection as another unknown field; the stationarity condition then selects the metric connection, just as stationarity selects the geodesic among trial curves.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Works cleanly only with a symmetric connection in more than two dimensions and with matter that does not couple to the connection independently.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: On a curved 2-surface the learner blends the Levi-Civita connection with an added symmetric tensor C via a slider; the app parallel-transports a vector around a loop, shows its length drifting when C is not zero, and displays the residual of the connection equation which vanishes only at C = 0.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A Lagrangian containing second derivatives of the metric must give fourth-order field equations.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: For sqrt(-g) R the second-derivative coefficient contains only undifferentiated metric, and the second derivatives can be packed into a total divergence, so the equations are second order.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The generic Euler-Lagrange formula (11.25) contains a double divergence of a term that could itself contain second derivatives.
concepts: second-order nature of the Einstein equations

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The divergence identity nabla_b L^ab = 0 holds only for solutions of the field equations.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: It holds identically for every metric, because it follows from invariance of the action under coordinate changes rather than from stationarity.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Most results obtained from a variational principle are on-shell statements.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A valid gravitational Lagrangian must itself be a scalar density.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The first-order Gamma-Gamma Lagrangian is not a scalar density but gives exactly the same field equations, since it differs from sqrt(-g) R by a divergence. Covariance lives in the equations, not necessarily in every equivalent Lagrangian.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: §11.2 explicitly required a weight +1 scalar density to form an invariant action.
concepts: total divergence ambiguity of a Lagrangian

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The connection must be assumed to be the Christoffel connection before a gravitational action can be written.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: In the Palatini approach the connection is an independent symmetric field and the connection field equation forces metric compatibility.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Earlier chapters work exclusively with the metric connection once it is introduced.
concepts: metric compatibility from the field equations

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The variation of the inverse metric is obtained by simply raising the indices of delta g_ab.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Varying the inverse metric gives delta g^ab = -g^ac g^bd delta g_cd. So delta(g^ab) is minus the object you get by raising both indices of delta g_ab with the unvaried metric. Leaving out that minus sign is the usual slip.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Index gymnastics with the metric normally raises indices without sign changes.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A connection variation is not a tensor because connections are not tensors.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The non-tensorial part of the transformation law is the same for both connections and cancels in the difference, so delta Gamma is a (1,2) tensor.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Learners remember firmly that Gamma is not a tensor.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The energy-momentum tensor can only be built by guessing physically reasonable expressions.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Given a matter Lagrangian, T^ab is defined systematically by its metric variation, normalized with a factor 2 to match the canonical tensor.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Chapter 12 first builds T_ab for dust and perfect fluids by physical reasoning. Only in §12.7-§12.8 do the authors contrast that ad hoc method with the variational route set up here.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The trivial Lagrangian sqrt(-g) is useless for physics.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: On its own it gives impossible equations, but added to sqrt(-g) R with coefficient 2 Lambda it produces the cosmological term (used in DIV ch13 §13.3).
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: §11.3 dismisses it as unable to serve as a physical theory.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Different choices of dynamical variable (g_ab, g^ab, gothic g^ab) give different theories.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: They change the Euler-Lagrange expression by invertible algebraic factors (e.g. -sqrt(-g) G^ab versus R_ab versus sqrt(-g) G_ab), so the solution sets coincide.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The resulting equations look different, e.g. G^ab = 0 versus R_ab = 0.

thought_experiments.name: Shaking the coordinates inside a region
thought_experiments.setup: Imagine relabelling spacetime points inside a region by an infinitesimal vector field that is zero on the boundary, and treat the resulting change in metric components as a variation of the field.
thought_experiments.lesson: Since nothing physical changed, the action cannot change for any metric; this forces the Euler-Lagrange tensor to be divergence-free identically, explaining the Bianchi identity and the four redundancies in Einstein's equations.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Animated grid warp inside a fixed boundary with a live readout of changed g_ab components and an unchanged action integral.

thought_experiments.name: Pretend the connection is unknown
thought_experiments.setup: Write the gravitational action with the metric and an unrelated symmetric connection, and ask the variational principle to decide both.
thought_experiments.lesson: The connection equation leaves only the Levi-Civita connection, so metric compatibility can be seen as dynamics rather than definition.
concepts: metric compatibility from the field equations
thought_experiments.app_idea: Connection slider on a sphere showing parallel transport with and without metric compatibility.

historical_notes.event: Palatini's name is attached both to the formula for the variation of the Riemann tensor and to the method of varying metric and connection independently. Own historical note, not in the book: Palatini's 1919 paper gave the curvature-variation identity. The independent metric-affine variation was introduced by Einstein in 1925, so calling it 'the Palatini approach' is a historical misattribution.
historical_notes.significance: Supplies the chapter's central tool and its most elegant derivation.

historical_notes.event: The authors state that their variational treatment follows Schrödinger's short book Space-time Structure.
historical_notes.significance: Identifies the pedagogical lineage of the chapter's sequence (identities, indirect variation, first-order Lagrangian, Palatini).

historical_notes.event: Eddington considered a gravitational theory based on the square of the Riemann tensor, set here as Exercise 11.12.
historical_notes.significance: An early example of an alternative, higher-curvature action treated with independent variables.

historical_notes.event: Hilbert obtained the field equations from a variational principle in the same year Einstein published them; this chapter calls sqrt(-g) R the Einstein Lagrangian and leaves the attribution to DIV ch13 §13.3.
historical_notes.significance: Explains why the Lagrangian is commonly called Einstein-Hilbert in other texts.

applications_and_observations.details: In four dimensions the symmetric tensor L^ab has 10 components, and nabla_b L^ab = 0 imposes 4 differential relations among them. That leaves 6 independent equations, while the 4 coordinate freedoms account for the other 4 metric functions. Chapter 11 does not do this count; DIV ch13 §13.2 does it for G_ab = 0.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: 10 components of g_ab; 4 identities; 4 coordinate functions; 6 genuinely dynamical equations (own count)

applications_and_observations.topic: Size of the Palatini variational problem (own estimate)
applications_and_observations.details: Treating a symmetric connection as independent in four dimensions adds 40 unknown functions to the 10 metric components; the connection equation (11.48) supplies 40 algebraic-differential conditions that fix all 40.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: 40 components of symmetric Gamma^a_bc; 10 of g_ab; 50 equations total (own count)

notation_and_conventions.convention: An equation marked with a starred equals sign holds only in a particular coordinate system, here geodesic coordinates at P.
R^a_bcd = partial_c Gamma^a_bd - partial_d Gamma^a_bc + Gamma^e_bd Gamma^a_ec - Gamma^e_bc Gamma^a_ed (6.40); Ricci by contracting first and third indices, R_bd = R^a_bad.
notation_and_conventions.notes: With these conventions and signature (+,-,-,-) the action uses +sqrt(-g) R and the field equations read G^ab = kappa T^ab with positive kappa.

notation_and_conventions.convention: A gothic tensor means the tensor multiplied by sqrt(-g), a weight +1 density; e.g. gothic g^ab = sqrt(-g) g^ab.
g_ab,c = partial_c g_ab and g_ab,cd for second derivatives; partial L / partial g_ab,cd means differentiation with respect to the second-derivative variable.
notation_and_conventions.notes: In (11.43) and (11.44) the ', c' is typeset as a subscript under the superscript of gothic g^ab in the denominator. It means differentiation with respect to gothic g^ab_,c. The OCR reading copy prints it as a loose ', c'.

notation_and_conventions.convention: delta X is a first-order variation; delta L / delta g_ab is the Euler-Lagrange derivative; an identically-equal sign marks results valid for all metrics.
L_G for the gravitational (Einstein) Lagrangian, L_M for matter, L-bar_G for the first-order equivalent Lagrangian.
I = integral of (L_G + 2 kappa L_M) dOmega and T^ab = (2/sqrt(-g)) delta L_M / delta g_ab; equivalently sqrt(-g) T_ab = -2 delta L_M / delta g^ab.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Some authors drop the 2 in both places, which leaves G^ab = kappa T^ab unchanged.

notation_and_conventions.item: Signature and sign of the scalar-field Lagrangian
notation_and_conventions.convention: With the book's signature (+,-,-,-) the scalar field Lagrangian in Exercise 11.13 is written -(1/2) g^cd phi_,c phi_,d + V(phi), and the canonical tensor carries a minus sign on its derivative term, so that Theta_00 is the positive energy density.
notation_and_conventions.notes: This is the overall negative of the usual particle-physics Lagrangian in the same signature; mixing sources can flip the sign of T_ab.

notation_and_conventions.convention: dOmega denotes the coordinate volume element and dS_b the coordinate surface element; densities of weight +1 supply the sqrt(-g).

margin_notes.summary: The authors call the complete brute-force Euler-Lagrange calculation of sqrt(-g) R an exercise only for the utterly devoted reader.
Integration-by-parts step of the identity derivation is flagged '(check)' for the reader to verify signs.
Warning that the first-order Lagrangian L-bar_G, though equivalent, is not a scalar density.
The authors note that other texts drop the 2 from both the action and the definition of T^ab. Because the two changes cancel, G^ab = kappa T^ab is unaffected.
Further reading: Schrödinger's Space-time Structure (1950) as the basis of the approach, and Choquet-Bruhat, DeWitt-Morette and Dillard-Bleick (1977) as a more modern source.

notable.summary: Verify to first order the change in metric components produced by an infinitesimal coordinate shift, recovering the symmetrized covariant derivative of the generator.
notable.why_notable: Supplies the one quoted step in the central identity argument of §11.2 and links to Killing's equation.

notable.summary: Recompute the variational derivative of the Einstein Lagrangian when the independent variables are gothic g^ab, gothic g_ab or g^ab, and state the identity each satisfies.
notable.why_notable: Shows concretely that different variable choices give algebraically equivalent equations with different-looking identities.

notable.summary: Prove that a continuous function integrating to zero over every region vanishes, and that a vector contracted to zero with every covector is zero.
notable.why_notable: Makes rigorous the two arbitrariness steps used repeatedly in the chapter.

notable.summary: A six-part guided derivation establishing (11.41), (11.46) and (11.36), relating derivatives of gothic g^ab to the connection, and computing the partial derivatives of the first-order Lagrangian.
notable.why_notable: Fills in all the skipped algebra of §11.6; note that parts (iii), (v) and (vi) contain misprints in the printed indices and a sign.

notable.summary: Starting from the symmetrized Palatini connection equation, show step by step that the covariant derivatives of gothic g^ab, sqrt(-g), g^ab and g_ab vanish, and conclude that the connection is the Christoffel connection.
notable.why_notable: Completes the key claim of §11.7; a good place to discover the dimension dependence of the argument.

notable.summary: Find the field equations of Eddington's Riemann-squared theory, treating the inverse metric and the Riemann tensor as independent variables.
notable.why_notable: Only exercise that leaves Einstein's theory, testing whether the framework has been understood beyond one Lagrangian.

notable.summary: For a scalar field with potential, compute the canonical energy-momentum tensor in flat spacetime, build the curved-spacetime Lagrangian by minimal coupling, derive the variational T_ab and check that the two agree in Minkowski space.

notable.why_notable: Justifies the factor 2 in (11.52) and previews Chapter 12; the printed index on Theta^c_a should be b.

notable.summary: Use geodesic coordinates to show that the variation of the metric connection is a covariant combination of derivatives of the metric variation.
notable.why_notable: Needed for matter Lagrangians with covariant derivatives and closes the loop with the method of §11.1.

difficulty.notes: Short but dense: nearly every line is an index manipulation with densities, variations and integration by parts, and many intermediate results are delegated to exercises. Conceptually the key ideas (off-shell identities from covariance, boundary terms, divergence ambiguity, connection as a dynamical field) are deep but stated tersely with almost no physical commentary. Readers need fluent command of Chapter 7 (densities, determinants, divergence theorem, Euler-Lagrange equations). Several misprints (a missing boundary symbol, a missing '= 0', exercise index errors) add friction.
